title: Generac Generator Cost Installed: $10K to $20K for Whole House
metaDescription: A whole house Generac generator usually costs $10,000 to $20,000 installed; the generator is often a third to half of that. Here is each line item on a quote.
intro:
A Generac whole-home standby system usually costs $10,000 to $20,000 installed, and the generator is only about a third to a half of that bill. Your fuel source, the distance between unit, gas meter and panel, and the size you choose move the total most. Below: unit prices by size, every installation line item, ownership costs, cheaper options and ways to trim a quote.

The figure that surprises most buyers is how little of a Generac standby invoice goes to the generator. Of a typical $10,000 to $20,000 installed total, the machine is often a third to a half. The balance pays for a transfer switch, an electrician, a gas fitter, a pad and permits, and sometimes a propane tank or a larger gas meter. Once you can name those pieces, you can read any quote and see where it can shrink.

sections.heading: Generac Generator Cost: The Short Answer
sections.body:
Budget $10,000 to $16,000 for the most common choice, a Guardian 22kW connected to existing natural gas, and $10,000 to $20,000 for whole-home standby in general. Homeowners and dealers commonly report straightforward 22kW jobs clustering around $12,000 to $15,000. A workable rule: take the unit price, add roughly the same again for installation, then plan on some upkeep every year. The installed ranges below are typical at the time of writing, and local labor and site conditions shift them a lot.

| System | Typical output | Typical unit only | Typical installed total | Usually covers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Portable plus transfer switch or interlock | 3-8kW | $1,000-$1,300 (GP8000E) | $1,500-$3,500 | Selected essential circuits, manual start |
| Guardian 10-14kW | 10-14kW | $3,200-$5,000 | $7,000-$11,000 | Essentials plus some comfort loads, maybe one AC |
| Guardian 18-22kW | 18-22kW | $4,900-$6,500 | $10,000-$16,000 | Most homes, including a central AC with load management |
| Guardian 24-26kW | 24-26kW | $6,500-$7,800 | $12,000-$19,000 | Larger homes, two AC systems with load management |
| Protector liquid-cooled | 30-60kW | $13,000-$25,000+ | $20,000-$40,000+ | Very large or all-electric homes, light commercial |

### Which tier do most homeowners land in?

The 18 to 22kW band. That is where the typical house with one or two central air systems ends up once a dealer runs the numbers, and it is why the 22kW figure shows up in so many quotes. The total rises fast when the job needs a long gas run, a propane tank installed from nothing, a panel or meter upgrade, or awkward site work.

### What does a quote far from these ranges mean?

A bid well under the pattern above usually omits something, so ask what is excluded before you get excited. A bid well over it deserves an itemized breakdown, line by line, before you sign anything. Section 3 lists every line you should expect to see.

sections.heading: How Much Does a Generac Generator Cost Without Installation?
sections.body:
A Guardian standby unit alone typically runs about $3,200 for the 10kW up to $7,800 for the 24 to 26kW models, with the liquid-cooled Protector line far higher. Treat those unit-only numbers as a guide: Generac sells standby generators through authorized dealers, and plenty of dealers will only quote an installed price. Regional differences and promotions can move the figures below by 10 to 15 percent or more.

It also helps to know that the Generac name covers three quite different product families. The portable generators are retail items you can pick up from a store shelf. The air-cooled Guardian standby units are the backbone of home backup: mounted permanently outside and wired to an automatic transfer switch. At the top sit the liquid-cooled Protector generators and the PWRcell battery systems.

| Model | Rated output (LP / NG) | Typical unit price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guardian 10kW | 10kW / 9kW | $3,200-$4,200 |
| Guardian 14kW | 14kW / 14kW | $4,200-$5,000 |
| Guardian 18kW | 18kW / 17kW | $4,900-$5,700 |
| Guardian 22kW | 22kW / 19.5kW | $5,500-$6,500 |
| Guardian 24-26kW | Up to 26kW on LP | $6,500-$7,800 |
| Protector QS liquid-cooled | 30-60kW | $13,000-$25,000+ |
| GP8000E portable | 8,000W running | $1,000-$1,300 |

### Why is a Generac rated lower on natural gas?

Air-cooled standby engines produce less power on natural gas than on propane, which is why the table lists two ratings. In practice a 22kW Guardian behaves like a 19.5kW machine on a natural gas line. Size your home right up to a model's propane rating, then feed it natural gas, and the safety margin you thought you had is gone.

### Why is the 22kW such a popular size?

Because prices do not climb in a straight line. Moving from 14 to 18 to 22kW costs relatively little, since those units share much of the same design, so the 22kW buys a lot of extra capacity for a modest premium. The largest air-cooled sizes, and above all the liquid-cooled Protector units, cost disproportionately more for each added kilowatt.

### Is the transfer switch included in the unit price?

Sometimes. Generac bundles the transfer switch with some generators and sells it separately with others. A 200-amp whole-house automatic transfer switch commonly adds about $600 to $1,500 for the hardware alone, and service-rated or smart-management versions cost more. When you compare unit prices, check that each one either includes the switch or leaves it out, so the comparison is fair.

sections.heading: How Much Does Generac Installation Cost?
sections.body:
Installation typically costs about as much as the generator itself, and on a difficult site it costs more. This is the part of the bill that varies most and catches homeowners off guard. A standby generator is a small construction project that touches electrical work, gas work and sometimes structural work, and each of those needs its own permit and inspection. A capable dealer coordinates the whole thing, and every trade on site shows up on your invoice.

Typical 22kW Install, Rough Shares

40-50%

Generator unit

10-15%

Automatic transfer switch

25-35%

Electrical and gas labor

5-10%

Pad, permits, startup, misc

| Line item | Typical range | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical labor and materials | $1,500-$4,000 | ATS install, wiring from generator to switch and panel |
| Gas piping (natural gas) | $500-$3,000 | Rises with distance from meter and pipe size needed |
| Gas meter or regulator upgrade | $0-$1,500 | Utility may need a larger meter for the extra load |
| Propane tank set (if no NG) | $1,500-$4,500 | Buried or above-ground 250-1,000 gallon tank plus lines |
| Pad and site prep | $200-$1,000 | Composite pad often included; gravel base or concrete extra |
| Permits and inspections | $100-$1,000 | Electrical, gas, sometimes zoning; varies widely |
| Startup, registration and walkthrough | $0-$500 | Often bundled; confirms warranty activation |

### What does the electrician do, and when does the panel add cost?

The electrician mounts the automatic transfer switch, usually beside the meter or main panel, and runs conductors from the generator to that switch. Trouble starts when the main panel is old, already full, or cannot accept a service-rated switch. In that case the electrician may advise replacing or upgrading it, a job that can add $1,500 to $4,000 by itself.

### Why can the gas work cost so much?

The price follows distance and capacity. A 22kW unit pulls a large volume of gas when it starts and while it runs, and the line already serving the house may be too small to supply it alongside a furnace and water heater. Fixing that can mean a bigger pipe run from the meter and, now and then, a request to the utility for a larger meter. A home with no natural gas needs a propane tank big enough for several days of runtime instead, which adds a substantial sum.

### How do placement rules change the price?

Where code lets the unit sit decides how long the wire and pipe runs are. Generac's air-cooled units are commonly allowed as close as 18 inches from the house where local code permits, with about 5 feet of clearance from windows, doors, vents and other openings. Local codes, utility rules and HOA requirements can force the generator farther out, and every extra foot lengthens both the electrical and gas runs. Ask the installer at the first visit where the unit can legally go.

READING A QUOTE

Get four separate numbers from every dealer.

Ask for the unit and transfer switch, the electrical labor and materials, the gas work, and the permits and site prep as their own lines. With those four figures side by side you can compare bids fairly, spot where a high quote is padded, and catch what a cheap one quietly dropped.

sections.heading: Why Do Generac Quotes Vary So Much?
sections.body:
Five things account for most of the gap between two quotes for the same generator: distance, fuel, the state of your electrical panel, where and when you buy, and the site itself. Each one is worth asking about before you compare totals.

### Distance between the meter, generator and panel

Every foot separating the gas meter, the generator and the electrical panel adds pipe, wire, trenching and labor. The cheapest install puts the unit right beside the meter and panel on the same wall. Put it on the far side of the house, or across a driveway, and the bill can grow by thousands.

### Natural gas versus propane

Having natural gas already at the street is a large head start. Without it you pay for a propane tank, its pad or burial, regulators and lines, and depending on your propane supplier you may lease the tank or buy it. Buried tanks cost more than above-ground ones, though many owners and HOAs prefer how they look.

### Panel condition and load management

Older panels, full panels, panels from brands with known problems and homes on 100-amp service may need work before any transfer switch goes in. Some installs also add a smart management module that sheds big loads, such as the air conditioner or an electric dryer, as the generator nears capacity. Each module typically adds a few hundred dollars installed.

### Region and season

Labor rates in some markets are double those in others, and demand surges after big storms. In the weeks after a hurricane or ice storm, quotes often run higher and lead times stretch. Permit fees and rules also differ widely, and some jurisdictions want a zoning review, proof of noise compliance or engineered drawings.

### The site itself

Slopes, rock, tree roots and narrow side yards all cost money, especially when a crew has to hand-carry a 400-pound unit or bring in a crane or extra hands to lift it over a fence. A reputable dealer visits the property before quoting. Treat any price given sight unseen with suspicion.

sections.heading: What Size Generac Do I Need, and How Do I Avoid Overpaying?
sections.body:
Size to your heaviest appliances, not your floor area. Dealers frequently suggest whole-house coverage, which suits many homes, but square footage on its own predicts very little. What counts is your biggest loads, how many air conditioning systems you run, whether the heat, water heater, range and dryer use gas or electricity, and whether a well pump is involved.

### When is 10 to 14kW enough?

When you only need essentials. A smaller Guardian paired with a transfer switch that serves selected circuits can run the refrigerator, freezer, furnace or boiler, sump pump, well pump, lights, internet and kitchen outlets, and frequently one smaller air conditioner as well. In a home with gas heat and gas appliances, that approach can save $2,000 to $4,000 compared with a whole-house unit.

### When do you need 18 to 26kW?

For whole-house coverage. The 22kW is the usual whole-house pick for typical homes with one or two central air systems. Adding Generac's load-management modules lets it keep the air conditioning on while stopping an electric dryer or a second compressor from overloading the generator. That pairing often allows a 22kW to handle a house that would otherwise call for a bigger model.

### What about all-electric homes?

This is where sizing, and the price, climbs. Electric heat strips, heat pump backup heat, an electric tank water heater and an electric range add up fast, and a whole-house plan can steer you toward a liquid-cooled unit. Before you accept that, ask whether load management, or agreeing to leave a few heavy appliances off during outages, would let an air-cooled unit cover the house. Our [outage generator guide](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) explains running and starting watts in more depth.

### How should a dealer work out the size?

With a real load calculation, ideally based on your utility bills or a check of the nameplates on your appliances. A quote that names a size without asking what is in the house is a guess, and those guesses tend to run high.

sections.heading: How Much Does a Generac Cost to Run and Maintain?
sections.body:
Plan on a few hundred dollars a year for upkeep, plus whatever fuel outages burn. The purchase is the large payment, but a standby unit keeps costing money afterward, and most of it is predictable: yearly maintenance, a battery every few years, the small amount of fuel used by the weekly exercise run, and the fuel consumed during real outages.

### What does annual maintenance include and cost?

Air-cooled Guardian units need fresh oil, a new oil filter, an air filter and spark plugs on a schedule set by both run hours and time, which typically means at least once a year. Dealer service visits commonly cost $200 to $400, and many dealers offer annual plans priced in a similar range. Skipping service invites a no-start at the worst moment and can complicate warranty claims. Service history is also what decides [how long a standby generator lasts](/how-long-does-a-generator-last/).

### How often does the battery need replacing?

The starting battery typically lasts three to five years and costs roughly $50 to $150 to replace, more if a technician fits it during a service call.

### How much fuel does the weekly exercise use?

Very little. The weekly self-test runs for a few minutes at low speed and burns a small amount of gas, usually a few dollars a month or less.

### How much fuel does an outage burn?

This is the cost that swings. According to typical Generac fuel consumption charts, a 22kW unit at about half load uses roughly 2 gallons of propane an hour, or a couple of hundred cubic feet of natural gas an hour. At recent propane prices that can mean well over $100 a day of continuous running, while natural gas usually costs much less per day. Most of the time a generator runs at lighter loads, so actual fuel bills are often lower.

| Ten-year cost item | Typical range |
| --- | --- |
| Installed 22kW system | $10,000-$16,000 |
| Annual maintenance, 10 years | $2,000-$4,000 |
| Batteries, 2 to 3 replacements | $150-$450 |
| Exercise fuel | $100-$500 |
| Outage fuel | Highly variable; often a few hundred dollars |

### What does the Generac warranty cover?

Guardian units carry Generac's standard five-year limited warranty, and you can buy extended coverage on top. In some cases the warranty can transfer to a buyer when you sell the house, but read the actual terms instead of assuming it will.

sections.heading: What Are Cheaper Alternatives to a Generac Standby Generator?
sections.body:
The cheapest workable backup for many homes with gas heat is a portable generator wired through an interlock or transfer switch, at roughly $1,500 to $3,500 all in. Other standby brands, battery systems and hybrid setups are worth pricing as well before you commit to a whole-house Generac.

### Are other standby brands cheaper?

Sometimes, depending on your local dealers. Kohler, Briggs and Stratton, Champion and Cummins all build home standby generators, and dealers near you may price one brand more sharply than another. Compare like for like: output on your fuel, transfer switch type, warranty length and the local dealer's service record. Generac's big advantage is its dealer network, yet in some areas that network is stretched thin, and a well-reviewed local Kohler or Briggs dealer can be the smarter choice.

### Will a portable generator with an interlock do the job?

For essentials in a home with gas heat, often yes. A large dual fuel or gasoline portable connected through an interlock or manual transfer switch installed by an electrician can run essential circuits for a total of roughly $1,500 to $3,500. In exchange you lose automatic starting and take on refueling, noise and the duty of placing it safely for carbon monoxide: outdoors, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away. Our [gas generator rankings](/best-gas-generator/) cover the strongest choices.

### Is battery backup cheaper than a Generac?

Portable power stations are, at a few hundred to a few thousand dollars; they run silently indoors and suit short outages and medical devices, as our [power station guide](/best-portable-power-station/) explains. Permanently installed home batteries, Generac's own PWRcell line included, typically cost as much as a standby generator or more while delivering less total outage runtime, though they pair well with solar. A battery-only system usually makes sense because of solar savings or time-of-use rates, not outage backup alone.

### What about a hybrid setup?

Combining a small standby unit for essentials with a portable power station for overnight medical loads can cost noticeably less than a whole-house generator while covering the loads that truly matter. Ask a dealer to price both a whole-house system and an essentials system so you can see the gap in dollars.

sections.heading: How Can You Lower a Generac Installation Quote?
sections.body:
The biggest savings come from comparing itemized bids, timing the purchase, shortening the runs and buying only the size you need. Here is how each works.

### Collect at least three itemized quotes

Dealers can differ by thousands of dollars on the same install. Ask each one to price the unit and switch, the electrical work, the gas work, and the permits and site prep separately, and to list what is excluded. Confirm every dealer is authorized for Generac warranty work and licensed for both electrical and gas, or that it subcontracts to licensed trades.

### Buy outside storm season

Demand and prices tend to climb after major outages, and lead times grow. Late fall through early spring, away from big weather events, is often a better window to negotiate and book the work. Manufacturer promotions, such as rebates or extended warranties, also appear from time to time.

### Shorten the wire and pipe runs

Siting the generator close to the gas meter and electrical panel, within code clearances, cuts both pipe and wire. Ask the installer to point out the cheapest legal spot and price it against the spot you would prefer. Moving the unit a few feet can save hundreds of dollars.

### Right-size and add load management

A 22kW fitted with load-shedding modules can often stand in for a larger unit, and an essentials system can stand in for a whole-house one. Either swap trims the price of the generator and frequently the installation too.

### Check rebates, programs and financing

Some utilities, municipalities and insurers offer rebates or discounts on backup power, especially for customers who rely on medical equipment. Fuel-burning generators generally do not qualify for federal clean-energy tax credits, so be wary of any salesperson who claims otherwise. Financing is offered almost everywhere; compare its interest rate with your other options before you sign.

sections.heading: Is a Generac Generator Worth the Money?
sections.body:
It is worth it when outages already cost you real money or put someone at risk. Tally what a long outage costs your household: a flooded finished basement after the sump pump quits, a burst pipe in a frozen house, a week of hotel nights, a freezer of spoiled food, lost income for a home-based business, or medical equipment that cannot lose power. If one or two of those have happened in the last few years, a standby generator often earns back its price in avoided losses and stress.

### Is standby safer than a portable?

Yes, it is the safest fuel-burning option. A standby unit is installed to clearance rules and inspected under a permit, it starts and connects through an automatic transfer switch that prevents backfeeding the grid, and it removes the urge to run a portable too close to the house in the middle of a storm. For older homeowners, people who travel and households with medical needs, those benefits are hard to price.

### Does a Generac add resale value?

Somewhat, but do not count on it. In outage-prone areas, buyers and appraisers tend to treat a standby generator as a desirable feature, yet you should not expect to recover the full installed cost at sale. Think of any resale boost as a bonus, not the reason to buy.

### When is a Generac not worth it?

When outages where you live are rare and brief, the house has gas heat, and a portable with a properly installed interlock, or a battery station, already covers what you need. Then it makes more sense to spend a fraction of the money on one of our [small generator picks](/best-small-generator-for-home/) or a mid-size portable, add CO alarms and an inlet, and keep the difference.

mistakes.title: Comparing lump-sum quotes
mistakes.body: One bottom-line number hides what each dealer actually included. One bid may fold in a panel upgrade while another quietly leaves out gas piping or permits. Ask every installer to split out the unit and switch, the electrical work, the gas work, and the permits and site prep, so padding and gaps show up at once.

mistakes.title: Sizing by square footage alone
mistakes.body: A 3,000 square foot house with gas heat and one air conditioner needs far less generator than a 2,000 square foot all-electric house. Insist on a load calculation built from your real appliances; paired with load management, it often lands on a smaller, cheaper unit than any square-footage rule of thumb would.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the gas supply
mistakes.body: A large standby unit needs enough gas flow. Undersized pipe, or a meter that cannot carry the combined household load, causes weak performance or failed starts under load. Confirm the quote includes a gas sizing check and, where needed, a larger line, a utility meter upgrade, or a propane tank sized for days of runtime.

mistakes.title: Skipping annual service
mistakes.body: A neglected standby unit may refuse to start when the grid fails, which wastes the five figures you spent on it. Book yearly service for oil, filters, plugs and a battery check, keep the space around the enclosure clear, and watch the app or controller for warnings between visits.

mistakes.title: Buying right after a big storm
mistakes.body: Demand jumps after major outages, and prices and wait times can jump with it. Rushed jobs and overbooked dealers make a fair comparison harder. Where you can, shop in a calm season, collect several bids, and get the install on the calendar well before hurricane or winter storm season arrives.

faqs.q: How much does a Generac 22kW cost installed?
faqs.a: A simple 22kW job on an existing natural gas line usually totals roughly $10,000 to $16,000, and the generator itself accounts for about $5,500 to $6,500 of it. Totals climb with long gas or electrical runs, a new propane tank, panel upgrades, load management modules or a hard site. Collect at least three itemized quotes, since bids for identical work differ widely.

faqs.q: Why does Generac installation cost so much?
faqs.a: Several trades share the job. An electrician installs the transfer switch and wiring, a gas fitter runs the piping and sometimes arranges a meter upgrade, the site is prepared for a pad, and each piece needs permits and inspections. That labor, material and coordination often matches or tops the price of the generator, particularly when the unit sits far from the meter and panel.

faqs.q: What size Generac do I need for my house?
faqs.a: Your appliances decide it more than your square footage does. Homes with gas heat and gas appliances often manage with 14 to 18kW for essentials, or 22kW for nearly everything. All-electric homes and houses with several air conditioners may need 24kW or more, or load management. Ask the dealer for a load calculation built from the appliances you actually own.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to run a Generac during an outage?
faqs.a: That depends on the fuel and the load. Running near half load, a 22kW burns roughly 2 gallons of propane an hour, which can pass $100 a day of nonstop running at typical propane prices. Natural gas usually costs far less per day. The weekly exercise cycle uses only a few dollars of fuel a month.

faqs.q: How much is annual Generac maintenance?
faqs.a: Expect roughly $200 to $400 a year for a dealer service visit covering oil, filters, spark plugs and a battery and system check, and many dealers sell yearly plans in that range. Budget roughly $50 to $150 for a new starting battery every three to five years, and an extra oil change may be due after a long outage.

faqs.q: Does a Generac generator qualify for a tax credit?
faqs.a: Usually not at the federal level, because fuel-burning generators generally fall outside the clean-energy tax credits. Some states, utilities, municipalities and insurers do offer rebates, discounts or medical-need programs for backup power, so ask locally. A medical necessity can affect tax treatment in some cases; get that answer from a tax professional, not from a sales pitch.

faqs.q: Can I install a Generac myself to save money?
faqs.a: In most places that is neither legal nor safe. A standby install means service-entrance electrical work, gas piping, and permits with inspections, and Generac's warranty typically calls for installation by qualified professionals. Doing your own site prep, such as clearing a path or leveling the area, may trim a little. Leave the electrical and gas connections to licensed trades.

bottomLine:
A typical Generac 22kW on natural gas comes to roughly $10,000 to $16,000 installed, more when propane, long runs or panel work enter the picture, and then a few hundred dollars a year to keep it ready. Less than half of that pays for the generator; the installation is where bids split apart and where careful shopping pays off.

Collect three itemized quotes, ask for a genuine load calculation, site the unit as close to the meter and panel as code permits, and try load management before paying for a bigger model. Where outages are short and infrequent, a portable on an interlock or a battery station may be the wiser use of the money.
